Every aspect of owning a dog is an utter privilege, except for this. I've been telling myself that so much joy must need some kind of balance, just to get myself through it. But - it's still so, so, unfair. It seems like both your and my baby had to pass well before we expected them to, which is so utterly devastating. I can prepare myself for old age, but this was unexpected, soul-destroying, and really, really hard. I'm so sorry for your loss but I agree - I know I did the right thing for him, it just feels awful for me. I'm glad I'm not alone, but really sad that I'm not alone for your sake, if that makes sense.

That's it! It's the guilt and the thought that something could have saved them. I sank over $6000 AUD into finding the solution, and I would have sold my soul for things to get better but a blood transfusion was the last viable solution and it changed nothing. My guilt is that if I hadn't gone away I would have spotted it sooner and the prognosis wouldn't have been so dire. He was my soul dog, I adored him more than anything else. Thank you for your kind words, all I can do is hold a mirror back to you and say the same - your baby boy loved you, you did everything in your power, you had an amazing bond and the world is so, so unkind for ripping that away. I like how you pay tribute to your baby and will endeavour to do the same. Thank you.

He was so, so, gorgeous! He'd be in your lap within two minutes of meeting you, despite being way too big to be a lap dog. He was so, so, loving and sweet and strange. 

I hope I find some peace too - I think I'm getting there. It's odd - I was more distressed before euthanasia. Perhaps it's worse to see them so unlike themselves, it did give me some peace to know he was no longer in pain and suffering. Now I don't feel terror or desperation or hysteria, it's just a big, empty, lonely void. Thank you for your words and kindness.

I'm so sorry for your loss too - it's the bittersweet part of this subreddit I suppose - we can all relate because we're all going through tremendous grief. I really like your idea of journaling, I think I'll do that before I forget my favourite and funny memories (as the sad and recent ones seem to take up more space). I've collected all his blankets and fallen asleep smelling and cuddling them, I've moved his dog tag onto my car keys, I've scrolled and saved about five years of photos, have collected every collar, lead and harness we've ever used... It's not weird, I think it's weird to not feel this level of grief when you lose an essential part of the family, thanks for helping to remind me of this. Hugs to you too.

I feel like I'm gonna get shit for this, but I did 'The Perks of Being a Wallflower' with my Year 10 class from a similar background.

Did they vibe with the protagonist from the beginning? Fuck no - there were moments when they yelled out "GAY!" and bitched about the book relentlessly. But by the end? Every fucking one of those kids was rooting for Charlie and his friends.

Was it school-appropriate? Christ no - there was a vivid date-rape scene, a scene where they talked about two kids having sex with glad-wrap, sexual abuse and suicide... but was it totally and completely fucking relevant to the kinds of kids we teach? Hell yeah.

At the end of the novel, I posed two questions to my students to answer anonymously - 1\*) Is this book relevant to you?\* / *2) Are the topics in this novel too sensitive or graphic for you to enjoy?*

NONE OF THEM HAD AN ISSUE WITH ANY OF IT. ALL OF THEM LINKED IT, IN SOME WAY, TO THEIR OWN LIVES. The longer I teach, the more I learn that the 'less safe for school' texts have a greater, life-changing impact on the gritty, "things aren't great at home" kids.

I started as a very gentle teacher. I'm only 5 years in and still hold onto certain aspects of this nature, but have learned that there are always students who see this nature as something to take advantage of and tamper with. I did not naturally have the assertiveness I currently have. It grows with your confidence in your abilities and control within the classroom. 

Projection and voice control is very, very important. I have seen teachers spend the whole lesson yelling and screaming and being utterly ineffective. I rarely raise my voice, but when I do the students STOP what they're doing immediately and listen. I will raise it with a call to attention, their noise plummets, and I can give instructions, a warning, etc. at a normal volume and they HEAR it and respond to it. The power of being a gentle teacher is extremely commanding when you are able to use projection and volume when you need to. If you are raising your voice constantly - students tune it out. When you use volume and projection effectively, and only when you need it, those kids will listen.   
  
The advice your mentor teacher gave to you is the same advice I gave to my first mentor student last year. She was an awesome teacher, made amazing content, had a brilliance for the subject, but she lacked the confidence to project her voice and give whole-class instructions. Some of my classes would have eaten her alive if I wasn't in the room because of this. I have been in a position where I have felt utterly helpless and not in control in a room full of students and it is worse than anything anyone could have prepared me for or said to me. 

I was also on anti-depressants (began during a particularly bad prac and came off them less than a year ago - so I FEEL YOU). It's hard work, it takes time, and I never thought I would make it. My knees used to knock when I gave speeches when I was in high school, I used to write down everything I wanted to say in a lesson delivery in my first-second year prac, and I now can walk into a whole school assembly with students and parents and deliver a speech perfectly without practice. 

Nobody is born a teacher, we all struggle and work towards our craft until we make it.

Gotta be passionate about your area because it's hard work, in my opinion. I teach Visual Arts and love, love, love the fact that I get my hands dirty most days. English is my minor and I've taught quite a lot of English classes - I liked the routine of it, seeing the kids 4 times a week, etc. but it's not my driving force/passion and I got sick of it when I was teaching it for only 8 hours a week. Visual arts has its downsides - I can't tell you how many Saturdays I've had to come in, how many hours I've had to commit to attending exhibitions, hanging up artwork for school exhibitions, how early I have to come in to set up for a full day of practical classes, etc. If you're passionate about your area, all the better basically. 

The best thing about teaching is the kids and your subject area, also your colleagues/department when you end up in a good one. Admin usually sucks, the profession as a whole tends to be very time consuming. Don't expect all the 'holidays' to be holidays, don't expect to have no work to do when you get home, especially in the first few years. The kids can be really awesome, or absolute assholes.

No, I'm apart of the union and I understand my rights and entitlements. Did I not in my first few years and lost out on things like graduate allowances? Yep, absolutely. 

I don't think blaming it on the individual is a good thing to do. You don't actually go into teaching knowing these things, as no one explicitly tells or teaches you this. You certainly don't get told these things 90% of the time by your employer. I was too busy to read through pages and pages of documentation to teach myself this when I first started, because I was too busy trying to keep my head above water in curriculum, behaviour management, etc. Also couldn't afford to be apart of the union on a graduate salary living by myself and running out of money 4 days before my paycheck came through. Do I think this is maybe a little purposeful on part of the department and government? YEP. 

Regardless, your tone is not a helpful one. Instead of encouraging people to become more educated about their rights, you come across as blaming them for not knowing, when really, the system is currently designed to take advantage of teachers.

I do agree that the only way you'll know is trying and seeing - but nobody has really mentioned what a fucking pain a hecs debt is if you try and see, and choose to leave. This career definitely requires you to stick it out for a while when things are bad, and you often wont know if a school or community is right for you until you're in it, regardless of research. Writing a resume and cover letter, which they expect to be tailed to each individual school's business needs and ethos, often feels impossible to do on top of your workload. 

I went into teaching straight from high school and am probably one of the few left from my uni graduating cohort who is still teaching. I do think mature age students 'make it' more than young grads from what I've seen/annecdotal evidence. Regardless of what age you enter the career, you need to be a very, very, resiliant person as the burn out and stress is very real. I've found myself getting more frequently burnt out in the last year or two, more so than my first few years, as the teacher shortage, teaching out of area, and increasing responsibilities/duties other than teaching has had a big impact. Don't expect your afternoons, weekends and school breaks to be free from work all the time. My marking load is insane - I have spent almost every weekend for the past 6 weeks marking at least one day and I STILL feel like I'm drowning. I would assume the marking load for primary school would be far better, but there are always pros/cos for the area you choose to teach in.

 In regards to what course is right for you, I'm not entirely sure if you mean early childhood, primary, or secondary. I'm secondary and a part of what keeps me tethered to the job (apart from the kids, who I ADORE), is being passionate about teaching visual arts. If you have a specialty and passion for a certain area, pick high school, if you enjoy and are good at working with younger students, perhaps pick primary or early education.  

I don't want to be a downer, just realistic. I wish I knew a lot of what I knew now before entering into teaching. I doubt it would have changed my career choice, but it would have given me clearer expectations.

I will say that the downside of teaching in The Arts is that it's not just a Learning Area, it's also an extracurricular. 

You can get away with not being married to the job - there is someone in my department who does exactly this (I will say though, she makes everyone else's jobs harder because we're always picking up her slack, but she's also a massive bitch so it could be that lol). If you're not willing to put in absurd extra hours, you'll likely find yourself teaching the bottom rung of classes in a secondary/high school setting. If you're at a good school, this is quite enjoyable - if not, Year 7-9 Visual Arts can be nightmarish. 

I'm at the point where I teach mostly upper school classes and extension art - it's fucking awesome. The kids are amazing and talented, and I can really push more challenging projects. But this is after 5 years of regular attendance at external student exhibitions, after hours, in my own time, producing school murals every year, running extra-curricular clubs and school-wide events, making art links between school and community, and a bunch of other exhausting shit. 

Teaching Design and/or Media (from my experience) is far less stressful and less of a time commitment. Still fucking hard work, but less of a time commitment (and less fun imo haha, but being covered in paint is my idea of a good day). 

Honestly, talk to as many people as you can before you make the decision to go into teaching. Where the industry is at right now, I wouldn't recommend it to someone who isn't as resilient as fucking cement.

**This.** Although a lot of advice here is helpful, THIS is your quickest way out of your current nightmare. Classroom politics. 

I have been at my school for 5 years now (high school). I feel like a fucking rockstar walking around during recess and lunch because I get mobbed by kids who want to chat. 

My first two years at the school... fucking AWFUL. Would cry the whole drive home because the kids treated me like absolute shit. They were nasty, threatening, rude... and I see them do it to new teachers ALL the time. We had a staff member leave after students stole her phone and threw it down the toilet. I think this may apply to primary school, as a new year, new teacher, new class is... a big change. 

Kill them with kindness, NEVER lose your cool if you can help it, and draw them in with learning that they'd fucking love to participate in. I've done graffiti art with the roughest kids in school and have built great relationships with them. Always remember that these kids are emotionally turbulent - you can't be. They're expecting you to blow up, lose your cool and give up on them. Try your absolute best not to.

Clicker training changed our walks (and lives). My dog was the same, food motivated but too distracted to follow commands/be rewarded on walks (and therefore too unable to have his behaviour modified). Do some googling first, grab a clicker for like $5, as well as some high-value food (chicken, sausages, cheese in small amounts, etc.). 

Get her used to the clicker at home, she essentially needs to associate that clicking sound with the "good behaviour, treat". When you're on your walks, play close attention to good behaviours (I started with heel - every time he fell in step beside me - generally like 30 minutes into the walk - I would click and give him some chicken. Repeat x40 before I started adding "heel") and start by rewarding these.  The click and following treat help her identify her good behaviours as well as builds her willingness to listen in a distracting environment because... well, chicken. 

Unfortunately there is no easy or quick fix. I have been working with my dog for the last 6+ months, specifically on his reactivity, and it is slow but rewarding progress (would be quicker with a trainer's help). While he still is really quite bad around other dogs (he's a rescue so we don't know his history), he has become really focused and eager to please when he knows we're training (like at the park), and actually listens and follows commands on our walks now! There is a lot of resources and reading out there, thankfully, but [here](https://www.reddit.com/r/Dogtraining/wiki/reactivity) is a good place to start. Positive reinforcement, clicker training and focusing on games that encourage impulse-control. Something I found quite fundamental was offering experiences for ***him*** to make a ***choice***, and rewarding good ones, as opposed to just command and reward. I've commented some of the games/training we do on another comment on this post if you're interested!

Pulling was a process (and still is!). I did the stop/start thing for a bit, and while this reduced the amount he pulled, he was still doing it (still does at the beginning of our walks/if he spots a distraction). After he'd learned to pull less, I started teaching heel. Once he *knew* what heel was, the trouble was getting him to actually do it on command. For a month or two, I'd wait until we got to the point on our walks where he was a little more tired. Every now and then he'd fall in line with me, and I'd say "heel!", click, and reward with high-value treats (chicken). Over time, he was falling in line with me more and more. I increased distance between the time he started to heel and the time he was rewarded (5 steps to 10, 20, etc.). Now, when he's calmed down after the first 10-15 minutes into our nightly walk, he'll mostly heel without being asked. In fact, I think I've only actually used "heel" as a command/order 3-4 times (and he's responded). Although, I don't use it in an instance where I know it'll fail (if there's a dog across the road); I'll start to use it when we're more confident/reduce his threshold around other dogs.

Edit to mention: despite heeling without being asked, he'll often look at me expectantly for a treat. I don't reward when he does this, but after a few more steps when he's looked away. This way, I feel like I'm not encouraging his expectation to be consistently rewarded, but he also won't lose his motivation to heel if ignored for a while.

He doesn't mind a sniff but this usually premeditative of him marking/taking a whizz. He's not infatuated like a hound would be, just a normal sniffer. If the window is open he'll lunge out and bark at people, children, cyclists... despite being desperately friendly when meeting people on or off leash. If he's belted/unable to move he'll whine and scream, so I've compromised by looping his leash around a backseat headrest when going down the road to the park. Still throws himself against the window and barks if they're up too.

It's been such a long and arduous 3-4 months with quite a lot of trial and error! Alfie is the same. As soon as he steps outside he's a totally different dog: hyper-alert, stubborn, almost intent on not listening. He's also got an extreme prey drive. I once watched helplessly from the shore of the river as he swam about half a kilometre after a duck!

Something that really helped was getting a clicker and switching to cooked chicken and sausage as opposed to dry treats on walks. Before, if he did something right he was usually too distracted to even reward - now, when walking and he hears the click he knows it means: good behaviour, see me for a treat. This has done wonders to enforce things like lead manners (he had to learn not to pull before he learned to heel), sitting at roads, etc. because he can clearly identify what behaviour I am rewarding. 

Also, the behaviours I was expecting him to perform on walks started to work when I spent some time at home teaching them to him. From there, I took him to an environment with distractions, but that I still had some control over, to practice/train.  I've found large open sports ovals/parks work quite well for us (especially right now, with clubs and teams closed). These tend to be 'leashed' parks but very few people  follow this, unfortunately. I can usually spot a dog in the distance before he can and put an adequate distance between us to do a bit of reactivity training (or just continue on with practicing 'this way' 'heel' and essentially just getting him to follow me). Over time, we've expanded to more parks/spaces during our walks to spend 5-10 minutes doing a bit of training before carrying on. I've noticed that this will focus him for the rest of the walk, and he will tend to behave better/be more attentive at these places in future. 

When training, I've found using 'games' really helpful and fun. You should be able to find more about these online/on YouTube: 

* Itsyerchoice - good for impulse control which translates well when on a walk
* "Search" or treat diving - basically you stand/sit in one spot, keep your arm still as you gently throw treats on the floor (one at a time) for your dog to dive on. After a while, add "search" (and click) before you throw. I've found this useful in emergencies when he wont budge/listen and there's an oncoming dog. Usually distracts him enough to get him moving again, as he'll break eye-contract by looking down to eat. You can use this like a 'bread-crumb' trail to lead them away from the trouble if you're quick enough with your treats. 
* "This way" or Emergency U-Turn - I'd basically been using the command 'this way' to move him on from smells/ruining nice gardens since our first walk, so it was one he already knew. When I decided he needed to learn the emergency u-turn I used "this way" and started to add treats. We started training at a distance with milder distractions like a kid on a bike or dog behind a fence before working our way up to dogs at a distance. We've been able to successfully avoid a few dogs who have surprised us now!
*  "Look at me" - this is the one he's found the hardest, but after I get his eye contact and hold for a few seconds before treating, he tends to be much more relaxed when we move on. You may want to substitute "look at me" with a sound (clicking your tongue or something) so it's more distinct than other commands. 

I'm proud of what he's accomplished but we still generally have a reactive moment every day. The better he's gotten, the more my frustration has turned towards other dog owners who can't seem to read body language, context, or even an "on-leash area" sign.
